title: Tilopa and Naropa
hookLine: the scholar Naropa leaves his university post to serve the wild teacher Tilopa

cards: Naropa had what scholars dream of. In the stories, he held a high post at Nalanda, a great monastic university in India, where he defended the teaching in debate and could recite texts by the shelf.
One day, as he sat reading, a shadow fell across the page. An old woman, bent and ugly in the telling, asked him a question. Do you understand the words, or the meaning?
Naropa said: the words. She laughed with delight. Then he added: and the meaning.

teach.b: In Tibetan tellings, the old woman is a dakini, a wisdom figure in disguise. Her laughter and her tears say it all: Naropa knew the words, but not yet the meaning. When he asked who did, she named Tilopa.
Naropa gave up his post and went looking, and the stories make it hard.
He finds Tilopa nowhere and everywhere: in strange people on the road who disgust him, whom he refuses to help, and who turn out, too late, to have been Tilopa all along.
When Naropa finally finds him, Tilopa looks nothing like a professor.

teach.h: A WILD TEACHER BY THE RIVER.
teach.b: In some tellings he's a wild man by a river, living on scraps of fish. He doesn't lecture. He sets Naropa trials, one after another, many of them painful and some frightening, and teaches through each one in a few words.
The legend is extreme, and Kagyu tellings hold it up as a picture of devotion to a teacher.
What it carries is a reversal: the celebrated scholar becomes the servant of someone with no titles, because that person knows the meaning.
In the Kagyu tradition, Tilopa and Naropa stand at the head of a lineage, teacher to student, that we'll follow over the coming days. Knowing the words is good.
Somewhere near you, someone with no credentials may know the meaning.

how: In the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, Tilopa and Naropa are honored at the head of the lineage, and the story of Naropa's search is told to students as a picture of devotion and of the gap between knowing words and knowing their meaning.

o: a court poet who mocks proud scholars
an old nun who teaches at a great monastery
a wisdom figure in disguise who tests the seeker

games.q: Tilopa and Naropa: tap the pairs.

s: the old woman laughed when Naropa said he understood the meaning
she laughed at 'the words' and wept at 'the meaning'.
Tilopa taught Naropa through trials rather than lectures
the stories have him teach through each trial, in a few words.
Naropa stopped to help each stranger on the road
he refused them, and each turned out to have been Tilopa.

games.q: you're Naropa. a stranger on the road is doing something that disgusts you and asks for your help. what do you do?
o: walk past; you have a teacher to find.
lecture the stranger on proper conduct.
games.why: in the stories Naropa walks past, again and again, and each stranger turns out to have been Tilopa.

practice: Let your mind move through people you'll meet today or met yesterday, the bus driver, a child, the person at the register, a neighbor you never talk to, and pause on one.
Ask what this person might know that you don't, and let the question sit, unanswered, as you come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Dakini. A wisdom figure in disguise, like the old woman whose question sent Naropa to find his teacher Tilopa. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the scholar served. Words first, and then the long road to their meaning. Until next time.
